text:
This spring Erlend and Kristin stayed at the town house over Easter and had the youngest child, Munan, with them, for there was a sister at Bakke convent who was so skilled a healer that every sick child placed in her hands recovered, unless it was God’s will that the child should die.

One day just after the holy days, Kristin came home from the convent with the little boy. The manservant and maid who had accompanied her came into the room with her. Erlend was there alone, lying on one of the benches. When the manservant had gone out and the women had taken off their cloaks—Kristin sat by the fire with the child, and the maid was warming some oil they had received from the nun—Erlend asked from where he lay what Sister Ragnhild had said about the child. Kristin gave short answers while she undid the swaddling clothes; at last she did not answer at all.

“Is the boy so ill, Kristin, that you will not tell me?” he asked, with some impatience in his tone.

“You have asked about this before, Erlend,” his wife answered coldly, “and I have explained it many times. But when you care so little about the boy that you cannot remember it from one day to the next—”

“It has happened to me too, Kristin,” said Erlend, rising and coming over to her, “that I have had to answer you twice and three times about something you yourself asked me, because you could not be bothered to remember what I answered—”

“It was surely not about matters as grave as the children’s health,” she said in the same manner as before.

“Nor was it about trifling news—this winter; those matters weighed heavily on my mind.”

“That is not true, Erlend. It is a year and a day since you spoke to me of the matters that weighed most heavily on your mind—”

“Go out, Signe,” Erlend said to the girl. His forehead had reddened; he turned to his wife. “I understand what you are hinting at. I will not speak of it with you while your maid listens—even if you are so close a friend of hers that you think nothing of having her present when you pick a quarrel with your husband and say that I speak falsely—”

“In time one learns the customs of those with whom one shares a dwelling,” Kristin said curtly.

“It is not easy to understand what you mean. I have never spoken unkindly to you where strangers could hear, nor forgotten to show you the honor and respect due you before our servants.”

Kristin burst into a strange, sick, trembling laugh.

“You forget well, Erlend! All these years Ulf Haldorssøn has lived with us. Do you remember when you had him and Haftor escort me to you in the sleeping loft at Brynhild’s in Oslo?”

Erlend sank down upon the bench and stared at his wife with his mouth half open. But she continued:

“Little has happened at Husaby—or elsewhere—of indecency and dishonor that you thought to conceal from your servants, whether it brought shame upon yourself or upon your wife—”

Erlend sat as before, looking at her in dismay.

“Do you remember the first winter we were married? I was carrying Naakkve; matters stood so that it could be difficult enough for me to demand obedience and respect from my household. Do you remember how you supported me? Do you remember when your foster father visited us with strange ladies and maids and men-at-arms, and our own people sat at table with us? Do you remember that Munan stripped from me every shred with which I might have covered myself, while you sat still and did not dare stop his mouth—?”

“Jesus! Have you carried and hoarded this for fifteen years!” Then he lifted his eyes to her; they looked strangely pale blue, and his voice was weak and helpless. “And yet, my Kristin—it does not seem to me the same as when the two of us speak unfriendly and spiteful words to each other—”

“No,” said Kristin. “It also cut more deeply into my heart that time at our Christmas feast when you reviled me because I had thrown my cloak over Margret—and ladies from three counties stood around and heard it—”

Erlend did not answer.

“And yet you blame me for what happened with Margret. Every time I tried to teach her with a single word, she ran to you, and with unfriendly words you ordered me to leave the maiden in peace—she was yours and not mine—”

“I have not blamed you!” Erlend answered laboriously, struggling hard to speak calmly. “If one of our children had been a daughter, perhaps you would more readily have understood that a thing such as this with my daughter—it pierces through a father to the marrow—”

“I thought I showed you last spring that I understood,” his wife said softly. “I needed only to remember my own father—”

“Nevertheless,” Erlend said, still calmly, “this was worse. I was an unmarried man. That other man—was—married. I was not bound—not bound in such a way,” he corrected himself, “that I could never be released—”

“And yet you did not release yourself,” said Kristin. “Do you remember how it came about that you were released?”

Erlend sprang up and struck her in the face. Afterward he stood aghast and stared; a red mark appeared on the white cheek. But she sat rigid and still, her eyes hard. The child had begun to cry in fright; she rocked him a little in her lap and hushed him.

“That—that was cruelly said, Kristin,” the man said uncertainly.

“The last time you struck me,” she said quietly, “I carried your child beneath my heart. Now you have struck me while I sat with your son in my lap—”

“Yes, we are forever having these children—” he cried impatiently.

They fell silent. Erlend began pacing rapidly up and down the floor. She carried the child into the inner chamber and laid him on the bed. When she appeared again in the doorway, he stopped before her.

“I—I should not have struck you, my Kristin. I wish I had not done it. I suppose I shall regret it as long as I regretted the last time. But you—you have told me before that you think I forget too easily. But you forget nothing—no wrong I have done you. I have tried—tried to be a good husband to you, but perhaps you do not think that worth remembering. You—you are beautiful, Kristin—” He watched her as she walked past him.

Ah, the housewife’s quiet and dignified bearing was as beautiful as the maiden’s supple grace had been. She was broader across the bosom and hips, but she was taller too; she held herself erect, and her neck bore the small round head proudly and beautifully. The pale, closed face with its large dark-gray eyes incited and inflamed him as much as the round, rosy child’s face had once incited and inflamed his restless spirit by its strange composure. He went over and took her hand.

“To me, Kristin, you will always be the most beautiful of all women, and the dearest—”

She let him hold her hand, but did not return its pressure. He flung it away; his temper mastered him again.

“Forgotten, you say I have. That is not always the greatest sin—to forget. I have never pretended to be a pious man, but I remember what Sira Jon taught me when I was a child, and God’s servants have reminded me of it since. It is a sin to brood over and remember the sins we have confessed to the priest, made amends for before God, and received His forgiveness for from the priest’s hand and mouth. And it is not out of piety, Kristin, that you forever tear open these old sins of ours; you wish to hold the knife against me whenever I cross you—”

He walked away from her and came back.

“Domineering—God knows that I love you, Kristin—even though I see that you are domineering, and you have never forgiven me for wronging you and enticing you into wrongdoing. I have endured much from you, Kristin, but I will no longer endure never being granted peace from these old misfortunes, nor that you speak to me as though I were your thrall—”

Kristin trembled with agitation as she answered:

“I have not spoken to you as though you were a thrall. Have you ever heard me speak harshly or angrily to any person who might be counted my inferior—even if it were the most incompetent and wretched of our servants? Before God, I know myself innocent of the sin of having offended His poor in word or deed. But you were to be my lord; you were the one I was to obey and honor, bow before and lean upon next to God—according to God’s law, Erlend! And if I have lost patience and spoken to you as it does not become a wife to speak to her husband, perhaps it was because many a time you made it difficult for me to submit my lack of understanding to your better judgment, to honor and obey my husband and lord as much as I most wished to—and perhaps I expected you—perhaps I thought I could provoke you into showing that you were the man and I only a poor woman—

“But take comfort, Erlend. I shall not offend you with words again, and from this day onward I shall never forget to speak to you as gently as though you were descended from thralls—”

Erlend’s face had become dark red. He raised his fist at her—then turned abruptly on his heel, seized his cloak and sword from the bench by the door, and rushed out.

Outside there was sunshine and a sharp wind—cold air, but bright sparks of frozen drops of thaw water were blown against him from the eaves and from the wind-tossed treetops. The snow on the roofs shone like silver, and behind the black-green wooded ridges surrounding the town, the mountains glittered cold blue and brilliant white in the keen, luminous day of winter turning toward spring.

Erlend strode through streets and alleys, swiftly and at random. He was seething within. She had been wrong, so plainly wrong from the beginning, and he had been right; then he had lost control of himself and struck her and diminished his right—but she had been wrong. He did not know where to go now. He had no desire to visit acquaintances, and he would not go home.
